tur61-2: In a 2019 Cochrane review covering 14 studies and 1,579 patients, exercise programmes lasting a median of 12 weeks, mostly added to medication, slightly improved day-to-day function and slightly reduced disease activity as rated by patients, compared with no exercise. Pain could also ease: pain scored at 6.2 out of 10 was about 2 points lower in those who exercised. In patients already receiving their usual care, exercise programmes probably added little or no benefit for function and pain; the measured differences were not clinically important.
tur61-3: When your hamstring muscles are strong enough. Returning too early can make the injury worse, while staying inactive for too long can lead to muscle wasting and scar tissue. Deciding when to return together with a physiotherapist or doctor is the safest approach. According to a 2023 international expert consensus, rehabilitation should progress according to the muscle's capacity and your symptoms; the acceptable level of pain depends on the activity, but sprinting should be pain-free. The decision to return to sport is based on the demands of match play and the athlete's capacity. In a Swedish study of 75 elite footballers, return to play took an average of 28 days with a programme based on exercises that work the muscle while it lengthens, and 51 days with a conventional programme.
tur61-4: In a Norwegian study of 554 people aged 18–60, non-surgical treatment, open surgery and minimally invasive surgery gave similar results after one year. The tendon re-ruptured in 6.2% of the non-surgical group and 0.6% of the surgical groups; nerve injury occurred in 0.6% of the non-surgical group, 2.8% after open surgery and 5.2% after minimally invasive surgery. Surgery is considered more often for late presentation (more than 2–3 weeks), re-rupture, the tendon pulling away from the bone and elite athletes. In a 2019 meta-analysis pooling 29 studies, surgery also meant fewer re-ruptures but more of other complications; in studies using early-movement (functional) rehabilitation, there was no significant difference in the re-rupture rate between the two groups. The decision is made with your doctor. For non-surgical treatment, the UKSTAR trial of 540 people at 39 hospitals in the UK found that a walking boot allowing immediate weight-bearing gave similar results to a plaster cast: function scores at 9 months did not differ, and re-rupture occurred in 5% of those treated with a boot and 6% of those treated with a cast.
